name: Coumarin (taken by mouth)
short: Liver failure (2 likely deaths, 1 transplant): French survey, 34 liver reactions (15 likely or probable) to medicinal coumarin, over half off its lymphoedema indication. Reviews: a subset susceptible.
text: A French pharmacovigilance survey of synthetic coumarin, a medicine registered in France for lymphoedema of the arm after breast cancer treatment but prescribed for other uses in more than half of the reported cases, examined 34 reported cases of raised liver tests and judged a causal relationship likely or probable in 15; reactions mostly appeared after 2 to 6 months, there were 14 cases of jaundice, 41% of patients were hospitalised, severe liver failure led to one liver transplant and likely to death in two other cases, and two positive rechallenges were reported; the abstract does not state the route. A 2022 narrative review describes the liver toxicity mainly as mild to moderate rises in liver enzymes, says only a few severe cases have been described in the literature with no reported cases of liver failure, and concludes it is restricted to a small subset of patients, possibly because of differences in liver enzyme (CYP450) metabolism; these two sources differ on whether liver failure has occurred. A toxicology review describes coumarin as having liver-toxic and cancer-causing properties, notes that a genetic-damage mechanism for the cancer effect was discounted by the European Food Safety Authority in 2004, reports that human clinical data showed a subgroup more susceptible to liver toxicity than the animals studied, and says dietary exposure comes mainly from cassia cinnamon, with heavy consumers able to reach the tolerable daily intake. In a retrospective study of 129 outpatients taking traditional Japanese medicines containing cinnamon bark, 76.0% had coumarin intakes above the tolerable daily intake, but abnormal liver test changes were no more common in that group (17.3%) than in those below it (19.4%). No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
